newsitem.title: USA: Americans would not panic if stock market dropped.
newsitem.headline: Americans would not panic if stock market dropped.

text.p: Some 54 percent of U.S. voters own stocks or mutual funds and 61 percent of these say they would not sell if the stock market dropped dramatically, according to a Reuters poll released Monday.
The poll of 1,008 registered voters, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby International Jan. 25-29, found participation in the stock market widely spread among income, ethnic and demographic groups.

The survey, which has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points, found 39 percent of those claiming an annual income of $15,000-$25,000 were in the market. That percentage rose along with income so that 90 percent of those earning $75,000 or more held stocks or mutual funds.
Around 58 percent of whites, 35 percent of Hispanics and 28 percent of blacks were in the market.

Asked what they would do if the market dropped dramatically, only four percent said they would sell their investments and get out of the market immediately, while 61 percent said they would retain their holdings as a long term investment, 18 percent said they would keep some and sell some and 17 percent said they did not know what they would do.

Respondents were asked how much they depended on the stock market for retirement. Some 24 percent answered that they were very much dependent on the market, 46 percent said they were somewhat dependent and 26 percent said not at all.
More than 79 percent of respondents said they had a savings account, but only 49 percent of Hispanics did so -- by far the lowest proportion of any group in the survey.

Only 65 percent of respondents said they currently had a retirement fund. Twenty six percent of whites said they did not have such a fund, compared to 46 percent of Hispanics and 51 percent of black respondents.

Not surprisingly, the more affluent had a much better chance of having a retirement fund. Only 31 percent of those earning less than $15,000 a year had such a fund, compared to 93 percent of those earning $55,000 or more. Only 36 percent of those who did not graduate from high school had retirement funds while 81 percent of those with college degrees did.

Around 77 percent of respondents had a credit card and even 49 percent of those earning less than $15,000 a year and 69 percent of those earning $15-25,000 had credit cards. In making monthly payments, seven percent said they paid only the minimum, while 34 percent said they paid something above the minimum and 54 percent said they paid their balance in full.
Respondents under the age of 30 were the most likely to pay only the minimum with 16 percent in this age group saying that is what they did.

Respondents were asked what they would do if they won $25,000 in a lottery. Almost a third said they would use the money to reduce their debts, 20 percent said they would invest it in stocks or mutual funds, 13 percent would put it in a savings account and 14 percent would spend it lavishly.
